Paltry means something is so small in amount, so weak in quality, or so worthless in value that it deserves to be looked down upon or dismissed with contempt. It's not just "small" or "bad" — it's small or bad to the point of being almost insulting or laughable.

That feeling of scorn or contempt is the soul of this word. Whenever you see or use "paltry," know that there is always a quiet sneer hiding inside it.
The Two Main Ways "Paltry" Is Used

1. A Paltry Amount (Quantity)

When "paltry" describes a quantity — usually of money, time, resources, or numbers — it means the amount is so meager or pathetically small that it fails to meet any reasonable expectation.

The company made billions in profit, yet gave its workers a paltry $200 bonus.

Here, $200 is not just small — it's embarrassingly small compared to what the company could have given. That gap between what is and what should be is exactly what "paltry" highlights.

More examples:

  • "After years of hard work, he received a paltry salary raise of 1%."
  • "Only a paltry number of people showed up to the event — just 8 out of 500 invited."
  • "She had a paltry two hours to finish a project that required two days."

2. A Paltry Effort, Excuse, or Thing (Quality)

When "paltry" describes the quality or significance of something, it means the thing is so feeble, trivial, or worthless that it barely deserves to be taken seriously.

He offered a paltry apology — just a quick "sorry" mumbled under his breath — after lying to her for months.

The apology exists, but it is so weak and inadequate that it's almost worse than nothing. "Paltry" captures that perfectly.

More examples:

  • "Her paltry excuse — 'I forgot' — did not impress anyone."
  • "He made a paltry effort to clean the house before the guests arrived."
  • "That was a paltry attempt at cooking — burnt rice and nothing else."
The Emotional Charge: Why "Paltry" Is Stronger Than "Small" or "Little"

This is the most important thing to understand about "paltry," and it's what separates it from ordinary words like small, little, or few.

Plain wordWhat it does
Small / Little / FewDescribes size or quantity. Neutral. No judgment.
PaltryDescribes size or quantity with contempt and disappointment.

Consider the difference:

  • "He gave me a small tip." → Simply states the tip was not large. No strong feeling.
  • "He gave me a paltry tip." → The tip was so small it was almost an insult. There is frustration and disdain in this sentence.

So when someone uses "paltry," they are not just reporting a fact — they are passing a judgment. They are saying: "This is beneath what is acceptable. This is not enough. This deserves to be looked down on."
The Register: When and Where Is It Used?

"Paltry" is a slightly formal word. You will find it more often in:

  • Written English (news articles, books, essays, formal speeches)
  • Situations where someone wants to sound sharp, critical, or emphatic

You would rarely hear it in casual everyday conversation. Someone might say "That's a pathetic amount" or "That's barely anything" in speech, but in writing, a journalist or an author might choose "paltry" for that added punch of precision and contempt.

These words share the spirit of "paltry" but have slight differences in flavor:

  • Meager — Focuses mainly on being insufficient in quantity. Less contemptuous than "paltry."
  • Measly — Very similar to "paltry," slightly more informal and almost humorous. "A measly five dollars."
  • Trifling — Emphasizes that something is so unimportant it's not worth attention. Often used for abstract things.
  • Negligible — Means so small it can practically be ignored. More neutral and technical than "paltry."
  • Pitiful / Pathetic — Very close in tone to "paltry," but these words often also carry a sense of sadness or pity.
  • Derisory — Especially used for amounts of money that are so low they invite mockery or ridicule. Very close to "paltry."

Among all these, "paltry" is special because it neatly combines both the sense of smallness/weakness and the sense of contempt in one clean, precise word.

A Few More Examples to Cement Your Understanding

• "The charity donated a paltry fraction of what it had collected — most of the money went to administrative fees."
  • "For a world-class tournament, the prize money was paltry — barely enough to cover travel costs."
  • "His paltry understanding of the topic was immediately exposed when the professor asked him a follow-up question."
  • "A paltry 3% of applicants were accepted — the competition was brutal."
  • "She dismissed his paltry objections and proceeded with the plan."

Paltry = so small, weak, or worthless that it deserves contempt — not just small, but insultingly small.

If you can feel that quiet sneer of disapproval every time you read or write "paltry," you have understood the word completely.
